t.2.18.1: To Kausalyā, the mother of Rāma, who was lamenting thus, the downcast Lakṣmaṇa then spoke words suited to the occasion.
t.2.18.2: This does not please me either, noble lady, that Rāghava, having fallen under the sway of a woman's words, should abandon the splendor of the kingdom and go to the forest.
t.2.18.3: Perverse, aged, and overpowered by the objects of the senses, what would a king not say when he is urged on and in the grip of desire?
t.2.18.4: I see no offense in him, nor any fault of such a kind, for which Rāghava should be banished from the kingdom to dwell in the forest.
t.2.18.5: I do not see that man in the world, even an enemy, even one who has been banished, who would speak of any fault of his, even behind his back.
t.2.18.6: Who, having regard for dharma, would abandon without cause a son who is like a god, upright, self-controlled, and kind even to his enemies?
t.2.18.7: What son, mindful of the conduct proper to kings, would take to heart these words coming from a king who has fallen back into childhood?
t.2.18.8: As long as no man yet knows of this matter, even now, together with me, take the government into your own hands.
t.2.18.9: O Rāghava, when you are guarded by me standing at your side with my bow, who is able to get the better of you, standing there like Kṛtānta himself?
t.2.18.11: Whoever is a partisan of Bharata, or whoever desires his welfare, all of these I shall slay, for the mild man is treated with contempt.
t.2.18.10: O bull among men, with my sharp arrows I will make this whole Ayodhyā empty of people, if it persists in what is hostile to you.
t.2.18.12: Once you and I have taken up the most bitter enmity, who would have the power to give the royal fortune to Bharata, O chastiser of enemies?
t.2.18.13: O queen, I am truly devoted to my brother with all my heart; I swear to you by truth, by my bow, and by the gifts I have given and the sacrifices I have performed.
t.2.18.14: If Rāma should enter a blazing fire or the forest, know, O queen, that I will have entered there before him.
t.2.18.15: By my valour I shall remove your sorrow, as the risen sun removes darkness. Let the queen behold my valour, and let Rāghava too behold it.
t.2.18.16: Having heard these words of the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Kausalyā, weeping and overwhelmed with grief, spoke to Rāma.
t.2.18.17: You have heard, my son, what your brother Lakṣmaṇa has said. Whatever is to follow upon this, do that, if it pleases you.
t.2.18.18: And you ought not, on hearing the unrighteous words spoken by my co-wife, to abandon me, burning with grief, and go away from here.
t.2.18.19: O knower of dharma, if you, most steadfast in righteousness, wish to practise dharma, then remain here and serve me, and so practise the highest dharma.
t.2.18.20: O son, Kāśyapa, living self-restrained in his own home and devotedly serving his mother, was endowed with supreme austerity and went to heaven.
t.2.18.22: Separated from you, I have no use for life or for happiness. With you, even eating grass would be better for me.
t.2.18.21: Just as the king is to be honoured by you with reverence, so too am I. I do not give you leave; you must not go from here to the forest.
t.2.18.23: If you go to the forest, abandoning me who am consumed by grief, I shall sit here fasting unto death, for I shall not be able to live.
t.2.18.25: Then Rāma, whose soul was devoted to dharma, spoke words in accord with dharma to his mother Kausalyā, who was lamenting thus in her distress.
t.2.18.24: Then, my son, because of this unrighteousness you will reach the hell renowned throughout the world, just as the ocean, lord of rivers, incurred the sin of slaying a brahmin.
t.2.18.26: I have not the power to transgress my father's word. I beseech you, bowing my head: I wish to go to the forest.
t.2.18.28: In our own family, long ago, at the command of their father Sagara, the sons of Sagara, while digging up the earth, met with a very great slaughter.
t.2.18.27: And the sage Kaṇḍu too, wise and knowing dharma, devoted to his vows, killed a cow in carrying out his father's command.
t.2.18.29: Reṇukā, his own mother, was cut down with an axe in the forest by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who was carrying out his father's command.
t.2.18.30: Indeed, it is not I alone who carry out this command of a father; this path, approved and trodden by those of old, is what I follow.
t.2.18.31: This, then, is what must be done by me, and it is done on earth in no other way; for no one who carries out his father's word ever comes to ruin.
t.2.18.33: For dharma is supreme in the world, and in dharma truth is firmly established. This excellent word of my father is grounded in dharma.
t.2.18.32: Having spoken thus to his mother, he then said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Lakṣmaṇa, I know your unsurpassed affection for me, yet you have not understood my intent regarding truth and self-restraint."
t.2.18.34: O hero, one who stands firm, taking refuge in dharma, must not make it vain once he has promised to fulfill the word of his father, his mother, or a brāhmaṇa.
t.2.18.35: I, therefore, shall not be able to transgress my father's command, for it is at my father's word, O hero, that I have been urged on by Kaikeyī.
t.2.18.36: Therefore abandon this ignoble resolve that rests on the warrior code; take refuge in dharma, not in harshness, and let my way of thinking be followed.
t.2.18.37: Having spoken thus to his brother out of affection, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, with joined palms and head bowed, spoke again to Kausalyā.
t.2.18.38: Grant me leave, O queen, as I go from here to the forest; by my very life you shall be adjured: perform the rites for my well-being. Having fulfilled my promise, I shall come back again from the forest to the city.
t.2.18.39: For I cannot, merely for the sake of a kingdom, set aside glory that leads to great prosperity. In this life that lasts so short a time, O queen, I will not today choose the lowly earth through unrighteousness.
t.2.18.40: That bull among men, soothing his mother and resolutely bent on going to the Daṇḍaka forest, then earnestly instructed his younger brother in his view and reverently circumambulated his mother in his heart.
